definition.text: A branch of statistics that deals with spatial or spatio-temporal data sets.

facts.text: It was first developed to predict the distribution of ore grades in mines and is now applied in soil science and in agriculture, especially precision farming.
Simpler interpolators such as inverse distance weighting came first; geostatistics goes further by treating values at unsampled places as correlated random variables.
A model of spatial continuity, often a parametric variogram, describes how strongly nearby values constrain the value at an unsampled point.
Using one spatial model across a whole area assumes stationarity, the same statistical properties everywhere; several methods relax that assumption.
It serves two goals: estimating the most likely value at each place, or simulating many alternative maps, called realizations, that together give probabilistic forecasts.
Bayesian inference plays a growing part, implementing kriging through a Gaussian process that is updated with Bayes' theorem.

definition.text: A graph or function describing how much pairs of observations differ according to the distance separating them, the key tool of geostatistics.

facts.text: Matheron defined the semivariogram in 1963 as half the average squared difference between values a distance h apart, the value being, for example, the iron content of soil.
Samples taken far apart vary more than samples taken close together.
Since nobody can sample everywhere, an empirical variogram is built from the squared differences between every pair of sample points, such as soil samples.
It is summarized by the nugget, a jump at the origin; the sill, its limit at large distances; and the range, where it nears the sill, often taken as 95% of it.
An empirical variogram is not guaranteed to be valid, so a model is fitted to it, most often linear, spherical, Gaussian or exponential.
The fitted variogram model sets the weights used in kriging.
Usage is muddled: some authors call the semivariogram a variogram, and the word semivariance can mislead.

definition.text: A geostatistical interpolation method that predicts a value at an unsampled point as a weighted average of nearby known values, based on a model of their covariance.

facts.text: Georges Matheron set out its theory in 1960, building on Danie Krige's thesis estimating gold grades from a few boreholes in South Africa's Witwatersrand.
Under suitable assumptions it gives the best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) at unsampled locations.
Ordinary kriging chooses weights that minimize the mean squared error, with the weights summing to 1 so the estimate is unbiased.
Its estimation variance grows as samples lie farther from the target point and depends on the sampling layout, not on the sample values.
Only one realization of the random function is ever observed, so kriging must assume some degree of stationarity to infer its statistics.
Variants include simple kriging with a known mean, ordinary kriging with an unknown local mean, universal kriging with a trend, indicator kriging and co-kriging of related variables.
Its basic form is computationally heavy, but approximations scale it to larger problems.

definition.text: A spatial prediction technique that regresses the target variable on auxiliary variables, such as terrain and remote-sensing layers, and then kriges the regression residuals.

facts.text: It is mathematically equivalent to universal kriging and kriging with external drift.
It implements Matheron's 1969 universal model of spatial variation, in which deterministic and stochastic parts of variation are modelled separately.
The trend is fitted by ordinary or generalized least squares, then the residuals are interpolated by kriging and added back.
Pure regression and pure kriging are special cases: with no spatial autocorrelation it reduces to multiple regression, and with no useful covariates to ordinary kriging.
It is used to map the spatial distribution of soil properties, provided covariate layers exist that correlate significantly with the property.
Covariates keep multiplying: near-global topography at about 90 m from the 2000 Shuttle Radar Topography Mission, and MODIS images at 250 m.
Odeh and colleagues named it regression-kriging in 1995; Minasny and McBratney call it the empirical BLUP.
Minasny and McBratney found that more, better data matter more than more sophisticated statistics.

definition.text: The way a quantity measured at different places takes different values from place to place.

facts.text: It can be described with spatial descriptive statistics such as the range.
Variability is not uncertainty: a perfectly known field still varies, and uncertainty depends on sampling as well as on the amount of variability.
Geostatistics has been used to study how pesticide sorption and degradation vary across a field.
Geostatistical descriptions carry their own uncertainty, since variograms can be uncertain and interpolation methods differ.
Precision agriculture studies variability within fields, such as how terrain and soil properties affect crop growth and water distribution.
Urban landscapes and golf courses show high spatial variability in soil composition, unlike uniform farm fields.

definition.text: Estimating the values of a quantity at arbitrary places from values known at a set of points, when the variables are spatial coordinates.

facts.text: Geostatistics uses it to build digital elevation models from spot heights or survey depths.
Methods for scattered points include nearest-neighbour and natural-neighbour schemes, inverse distance weighting, kriging variants and thin-plate or other splines.
Gridding converts irregularly spaced data into a regular grid.
GIS software produces interpolated surfaces with methods such as inverse distance weighting, kriging, splines and trend surfaces.

definition.text: A deterministic interpolation method that estimates unknown values as a weighted average of known points, each weighted by the inverse of its distance.

facts.text: Donald Shepard, a Harvard freshman, published the method in 1968 while overhauling the interpolation in the SYMAP mapping program.
Shepard tested exponents of distance and settled near -2, close to the gravity model.
It was among the simpler interpolators known before geostatistics.
In Slovenia's Idrija area, it was used in GIS to turn soil samples into a raster map of mercury concentration.

definition.text: The science of measuring the shape of the land surface and the effects of that shape on human and natural processes.

facts.text: It extracts surface parameters and objects such as watersheds, stream networks and landforms from digital elevation models.
These parameters improve the mapping and modelling of soils, and serve precision agriculture and soil-landscape modelling.
Thanks largely to the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission and lidar, elevation models now cover almost all of Earth at 100 m resolution or better.
Slope, how steep the surface is, and aspect, the direction the slope faces, are its most basic derivatives.
Slope is computed from a raster model by discrete derivatives; the Horn method uses a cell and its eight neighbours.
Because water flows downhill, surface derivatives can predict surface stream flow.
Its ideas go back to Brisson (1808) and Gauss (1827), but it grew mainly with GIS and elevation data sets from the 1970s.

definition.text: A steady-state wetness index, computed from slope and upslope contributing area, that quantifies topographic control on hydrological processes.

facts.text: It combines the upslope area draining through a point per unit contour length with the local slope in radians.
Beven and Kirkby developed it within the TOPMODEL runoff model; it was designed for hillslope catenas and is not meaningful on flat ground.
It correlates highly with soil attributes such as horizon depth, silt percentage, organic matter content and phosphorus.
Areas with similar values become saturated under similar moisture conditions.

definition.text: A widely used remote-sensing measure of the health and density of vegetation, calculated from the red and near-infrared bands.

facts.text: Values run from -1 to 1: near zero means little or no vegetation, negative values mean water or non-land, and high values mean dense healthy vegetation.
Chlorophyll strongly absorbs visible light from 400 to 700 nm, while leaf cell structure strongly reflects near-infrared from 700 to 1100 nm.
Bare soils give small positive values of about 0.1 to 0.2, and because wet soil darkens, soil moisture changes can shift the index without any change in vegetation.
Alternatives such as the soil-adjusted vegetation index and the enhanced vegetation index correct for soil background effects.

definition.text: Imaging that captures data in a small number of separate wavelength bands, typically 3 to 15, including bands beyond visible light.

facts.text: Hyperspectral imaging differs by using often hundreds of contiguous bands.
A single multispectral image can show water depth, vegetation cover and soil moisture content.
Mid-infrared bands at 1550–1750 nm image vegetation and soil moisture, and far-infrared bands at 2080–2350 nm image soil, silicates and clays.
Surface and subsurface soil differ spectrally; disturbed soil emits more at 8.5 to 9.5 micrometres, which helps detect buried land mines.

definition.text: Imaging that records a full, finely resolved spectrum across many continuous bands for each pixel, to identify materials or detect processes.

facts.text: Materials leave characteristic spectral signatures that allow them to be identified.
Sensors on aircraft, satellites or drones are used to investigate plants and soils remotely, assessing ground cover and soil chemistry.
In farming it is being used to detect the nutrient and water status of wheat and heavy-metal stress in plants.
Although often treated as a surface technique, it can probe beneath the surface, to a depth set by the spectral range and the sample.

definition.text: A spectroscopic method using the near-infrared part of the spectrum, from 780 nm to 2500 nm.

facts.text: It rests on weak overtone and combination vibrations, so light penetrates deep into a sample and bulk material can be probed with little preparation.
Its broad, overlapping bands require multivariate calibration, such as principal components or partial least squares, built on carefully chosen calibration samples.
Karl Norris at the USDA pioneered it for agricultural products in the 1980s; it is valued as accurate, rapid, non-destructive and inexpensive.
Soil-testing laboratories may use near-infrared scanning.

definition.text: A geophysical method that images the subsurface with radar pulses, recording reflections from buried boundaries.

facts.text: It uses radio waves usually between 10 MHz and 2.6 GHz, reflected where materials of different permittivity meet.
It can reach up to 15 m in dry sandy soils but only a few centimetres in moist or clay-rich soils; higher frequencies trade penetration for resolution.
Clay soils and salt-contaminated soils limit it most, and rocky soils scatter the signal.
It is used to study soils and bedrock, and cross-borehole radar assesses the presence and amount of soil water.

definition.text: A geophysical technique that images subsurface structure from electrical resistivity measured with electrodes at the surface or in boreholes.

facts.text: Current is passed between two outer electrodes in a line of four, voltage is read between the inner two, and a geometric factor converts the result to apparent resistivity.
Wetter soil is less resistive, dry and saturated soil can differ by orders of magnitude, and clays conduct through charged particle surfaces as well as pore water.
Electrode spacings of 0.75 to 12.0 m serve shallow surveys under 10 m, and depth is usually less than the widest spacing.
It maps soil moisture for precision agriculture, images root zones and tracks contaminants in soil and groundwater.

definition.text: The use of orbiting gamma-ray spectrometers to map the elements of planetary surfaces, especially the Moon and Mars.

facts.text: Cosmic rays strike nuclei in the soil, releasing neutrons and exciting nuclei that then emit gamma rays of characteristic energy.
The energy of each emission line identifies an element and its intensity gives the concentration; about 20 elements can be measured.
Neutron detectors sense hydrogen in the upper metre of the surface, revealing water ice; Mars Odyssey carried one with two neutron detectors.
Mapping from orbit fails for bodies with thick atmospheres such as Earth and Venus.

definition.text: A system for automated global soil mapping based on models fitted to soil profiles and environmental covariate data.

facts.text: ISRIC produces its world maps of soil properties at 250 m cells, with quantified uncertainty, by machine learning on the WoSIS profile database and over 400 global covariates.
It and the WoSIS database are ISRIC's flagship soil information products.

verification.title: SoilGrids 2.0: producing soil information for the globe with quantified spatial uncertainty
verification.evidence: SoilGrids produces maps of soil properties for the entire globe at medium spatial resolution (250 m cell size) using state-of-the-art machine learning methods to generate the necessary models.
